content: The core of a coronary guidewire plays a critical role in determining the device's performance characteristics. Typically, the core is tapered towards the distal end, where the tip is attached. If the tapering of the core occurs closer to the tip, the guidewire becomes stiffer, more steerable, and offers better torque control. Conversely, if the tapering occurs more proximally, it allows for a longer and more flexible tip. The core can either be continuous or joined. A joined core is more prone to bending or prolapsing when the guidewire is advanced. Guidewire cores made of stainless steel are stiffer, provide greater support, and offer superior torque control. On the other hand, guidewire cores made of nitinol are significantly more flexible. Guidewire Core Composition The core of a guidewire can be composed of nitinol, stainless steel, or similar metals. Nitinol Guidewire Cores Nitinol cores are designed with a super-elastic alloy that resists kinking. They exhibit excellent flexibility and steering capabilities, are likely more durable, and offer better trackability with reduced prolapse. However, nitinol guidewires may be less torquable and can store torque without effectively transmitting it to the tip. Single nitinol core wires sometimes wind up, storing torque rather than delivering it. Clinical Scenarios for Nitinol Cores Due to their flexibility and durability, nitinol-core coronary guidewires are particularly useful for navigating retroflexed circumflex coronary arteries. Stainless Steel Guidewire Cores Stainless steel was the original material used for coronary guidewire cores. These cores provide superior pushability, support, torquability, and shape retention, especially in core-to-tip designs.
